summary:
Formats output for the current player. The complete format is %[flag][width][.precision]type.

The following format controls are supported; flag controls can be combined.

Flags

" "     For integers or floating-point numbers, prefix positive values with a space and negative values with a minus sign.
"+"     For integers or floating-point numbers, always display a sign. Without this flag, only negative numbers have a sign.
"-"     Left-align the result. Otherwise the default alignment is right alignment.
"|"     Center the result in its field.
"="     For strings longer than the field width, use column mode and wrap the string automatically.
"#"     For strings, use table mode to output a list of words with line breaks ('\n') within the field.
"0"     Immediately precedes the width integer and pads unused field space with zeros up to the specified width.
"'X'"   Pad the field with the character in single quotes instead of the default space. If both zero padding and character padding are specified, the later specification wins. To pad with a single quote, double quote, or backslash, use the escapes "\'", "\"" or "\\".
"@"     The argument is an array; apply the remaining format controls to each element.

Minimum output width

An integer specifies the minimum field width. Use '*' to obtain the width from the output argument list. Values wider than the requested field use their actual width; shorter values are padded with spaces or zeros.
Width follows strwidth(): English characters have width 1 and Chinese characters width 2.

Precision

"." followed by an integer specifies precision. Ordinary strings are truncated at that length. If precision exceeds the field width, the field width becomes the precision. In table mode, precision gives the number of columns; if omitted, table mode calculates the best result.
":" followed by an integer specifies both field width and precision. A leading 0 uses zero padding instead of spaces.

Type

%       Output a literal percent sign, for example: printf("%%");
O       Format an argument as an LPC value; any type can be displayed, which is useful for debugging.
s       Format a string.
d, i    Format an integer as signed decimal; i is the older notation.
c       Format an integer as a character.
o       Format an integer as unsigned octal, without a leading 0.
x       Format an integer as unsigned hexadecimal, without 0x, using lowercase a-f.
X       Format an integer as unsigned hexadecimal, without 0x, using uppercase A-F.
f       Format a floating-point number.
